comments.author: @GeoRust1
comments.text:
This was a pretty good interview, I was surprised! 

I’m probably what one would consider a doomer. I try to be as holistic as possible however. I don’t agree that “we all die in 5 years” is a leap. I do agree that there are plenty of intelligent, “stand to reason” doomer arguments that will fail to be actualized in the real-world. I think that there is plenty of rationalization occurring. But I would not say that ‘all of us dying’ is outrageous whatsoever. I do think it can be harmful to label such a notion as extremism. There are plenty avenues and scenarios in which we all die.. *plenty*. We’re simply dealing with a superior transcendent technology for which has an exponential magnitude of effect in comparison to previous technology. This shouldn’t be an argument. 

I also don’t think that (p)doom is ridiculous. Obviously predictions are subject to ambiguity, and specific predictions are almost always inaccurate. But having 100% (p)doom is a reasonable stance. It’s not outside the realm of possibility that alignment of ASI is (literally) impossible. This would be a reasonable argument to make for 100% (p)doom. I’m not saying that such an argument is true by any means —I don’t know and I don’t think anyone does— but it certainly could be true, and so I don’t agree that it is a ridiculous opinion to have a (p)doom of 100%. 

Just my 2cents

This is not so. All do not do this. Just because you have not read the ones that don't treat artificial intelligence this way (or you have read them and not noticed) doesn't mean that they don't exist. You are selling science fiction short on this. Even in the early Isaac Asimov stories, when Multivac becomes self-aware it is made clear that this is an emergent property of a large computational system. It becomes self-aware as a side effect of its computational capacity exceeding a certain threshold, not because it was meticulously crafted to become self-aware.
